extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methods for determining stability/asymptotic stability of equilibria and for classifying flow behavior (gradient and Hamiltonian systems), including Lyapunov functions, invariance principles, linearization tests, and phase-portrait construction. Intended as textbook guidance and theorems used to prove stability and estimate basins of attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearization (eigenvalue) test for equilibria
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the linearization DF(X*) at an equilibrium X*; use eigenvalues of the linearization to infer local behavior: eigenvalues with positive real part indicate instability; eigenvalues with negative real parts indicate (linear) asymptotic stability; zero or purely imaginary eigenvalues leave the question inconclusive (origin not hyperbolic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for the pendulum linearization gives pure imaginary eigenvalues when damping b = 0 (inconclusive), or negative real parts when b > 0 (asymptotically stable). If the linearization has a zero eigenvalue (or purely imaginary pair), look for nonlinear methods (Lyapunov functions, invariance) because the linear test is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive-definite Lyapunov function implies stability
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists a C^1 function L: U → R with L(X*) = 0, L(X) > 0 for X ≠ X* (positive definite) on a neighborhood U and ˙L(X) ≤ 0 along solutions, then X* is stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses sublevel sets: choose δ so closed ball B_δ(X*) ⊂ U, let α be min of L on sphere, then U={X∈B_δ | L(X)<α} is invariant (L nonincreasing) so solutions starting in U stay in B_δ. Use quadratic Lyapunov candidates (ax^2+by^2+cz^2) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict Lyapunov decrease yields asymptotic stability
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is positive definite and ˙L(X) < 0 for all X ∈ U \\ {X*} (strictly decreasing along nontrivial solutions), then X* is asymptotically stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analytic proof shows that any solution starting near X* has no limit point other than X*. Lasalle’s principle (below) generalizes this by allowing ˙L ≤ 0 combined with invariance conditions to conclude asymptotic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of quadratic Lyapunov functions (practical approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: For many systems try L(x) = a x^2 + b y^2 + c z^2 with positive a,b,c and compute ˙L to choose coefficients so that ˙L ≤ 0 (or < 0) in a region of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in text: choose a = 1, b = 2, c = 1 to arrange ˙L ≤ 0; when a system parameter equals zero this choice can yield ˙L = -2 z^4 ≤ 0 showing stability. Use such trial quadratic forms as a first attempt; if unsuccessful, try more tailored Lyapunov candidates (energy functions, higher-order forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lasalle’s Invariance Principle (criterion for asymptotic stability and basin estimates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let L be a Lyapunov function on neighborhood U of equilibrium X*. If P ⊂ U is a closed, positively invariant neighborhood of X* and there is no entire solution in P\{X*} on which L is constant, then X* is asymptotically stable and P is contained in its basin of attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sublevel sets of L intersected with trapping constraints to build P (e.g. Pc = {E ≤ c and |θ|<π} for the damped pendulum). To apply check: (1) P closed, (2) positively invariant (use ˙L ≤ 0), (3) rule out nontrivial entire solutions with L constant (usually by showing equality condition forces equilibrium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy or Hamiltonian functions as (Lyapunov) tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Total energy E or Hamiltonian H often serves as a first integral (˙H ≡ 0 for Hamiltonian systems) or as a Lyapunov function when dissipation is present (e.g. for damped systems ˙E ≤ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the undamped pendulum E is constant along solutions (˙E ≡ 0) and level curves of E give the phase portrait. For the damped pendulum ˙E = -b v^2 ≤ 0 so E is a Lyapunov function; use its sublevel sets and level curves to infer stability and basins without solving the ODEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using sublevel sets and invariance to estimate basins of attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Define sets Pc = {X | L(X) ≤ c} (possibly with additional constraints) and show they are positively invariant; if Lasalle’s conditions hold then Pc is contained in basin of attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for damped pendulum choose 0 < c < 2 and Pc = {E ≤ c and |θ|<π}; show Pc positively invariant via ˙E ≤ 0 and boundary energy estimates; then Lasalle implies Pc ⊂ basin of (0,0). Sublevel sets provide constructive estimates of basin size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant and positively invariant sets (trapping regions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set P is invariant if φ_t(X) ∈ P for all t ∈ R for each X ∈ P; positively invariant if φ_t(X) ∈ P for all t ≥ 0. Such sets trap trajectories and are essential for long-term behavior analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use invariance to localize dynamics and apply Lasalle/Poincaré–Bendixson. For example, planes z = nπ are invariant in a model, and the region |z| < π is invariant so trajectories cannot leave it; this is used to show asymptotic stability within the region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradient system criteria (V as Lyapunov function)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X' = -grad V(X): ˙V(X) = -|grad V(X)|^2 ≤ 0, with ˙V = 0 iff grad V = 0. Critical points of V are equilibrium points; an isolated minimum of V is an asymptotically stable equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret geometrically: trajectories move downhill on V, level sets are orthogonal to grad V. Use V’s level surfaces to draw flow and to infer limit behavior; no nonconstant solution can have V constant unless it is equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearization of gradient systems: symmetric Jacobian → real eigenvalues
rubrics_metrics.description: At an equilibrium X*, the linearization matrix for X' = -grad V is the negative Hessian matrix (-∂^2 V/∂xi∂xj) which is symmetric, hence has only real eigenvalues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: gradient flows have no conjugate-complex-eigenvalue oscillatory linear behavior near equilibria; this informs qualitative classification (sinks/saddles) in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamiltonian system criteria in R^2 (conservation and portrait by level sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: For planar Hamiltonian X' = (∂H/∂y, -∂H/∂x): H is constant along solutions (˙H ≡ 0); equilibria are critical points of H; solution curves lie on level sets H = const.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot level sets of H and determine directions from vector field to obtain phase portrait without solving ODEs. Note conservative nature: H constant prevents asymptotic stability caused purely by H (no dissipation). At planar equilibria eigenvalues come in ±λ or ±iλ pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit-set properties and classification (α/ω-limit sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: ω-limit and α-limit sets are closed, invariant sets; if two points lie on same trajectory they have the same α/ω-limit sets; a closed positively invariant set D contains ω(Z) for each Z ∈ D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these properties to reason about long-term behavior: e.g. in the plane closed bounded limit sets that contain no equilibria must be periodic orbits (Poincaré–Bendixson); examples show ω-limits can be sets of equilibria joined by heteroclinic orbits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré–Bendixson restriction for planar flows
rubrics_metrics.description: In the plane, a closed, bounded limit set that contains no equilibria must be a closed orbit (periodic solution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem strongly restricts possible α/ω-limit behavior in two dimensions compared with higher dimensions. Use together with invariance and Lyapunov/sublevel sets to conclude existence of periodic orbits or convergence to equilibria.
